catalog_quote: Stressed syllables are realized as louder and longer than unstressed syllables. Stress in Tayap is generally not phonemic, and unpredictable stress occurs rarely. In the dictionary, unpredictable stress occurs on roughly two percent of words. Stress usually falls on the final syllable of an uninflected word (but see below for more information about stress on bound morphemes): ambagái ‘men’s house’ ... karép ‘moon’ ... koŋgód ‘hour glass drum’ ... makatók ‘green coconut’ ... toŋgodíp ‘Malay apple’ ... There are a number of non-predictable exceptions to the syllable-final rule. The orthography used in this grammar and dictionary marks stress explicitly on those exceptional words. Examples of two-syllable words with non-final stress: mbímaŋ ‘leech’ símbu ‘maggot’ ... Syllables with unpredictable stress are far more common with the vowel a than the other vowels. ... sources.quote: 'Stress is predictable in Taiap. When a morpheme consists of two or three syllables, stress is generally placed on the second syllable. Stress placement in the verb is somewhat variable, depending on which suffixes are affixed to the verb stem.' (Same page treats a-tukun 'eat' vs aa-tukun 'chop' as a vowel-LENGTH contrast, which the 2019 grammar p. 38 reanalyses as a STRESS minimal pair atukún vs átukun.)
sources.note: Only other Glottolog descriptive source; earlier preliminary analysis by the same first author says 'second syllable' of 2-3-syllable morphemes rather than 'final' -- agrees on predictable stress and on disyllables, diverges for trisyllables; superseded by the 2019 grammar (which lists trisyllabic final-stress forms ambagái, makatók, toŋgodíp and treats second-syllable trisyllables like atáwo, emári as lexical exceptions). Worth a one-line 'earlier analysis' note in the record, not a reclassify.
